abstracts.abstract: The exponential growth of user-generated multimedia content has fundamentally challenged traditional approaches to semantic content analysis, which predominantly rely on data-intensive supervised paradigms lacking rigorous theoretical foundations. This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic framework that reconceptualizes semantic multimedia understanding as an optimal compression problem, fundamentally shifting from empirical risk minimization to principled representation learning. By establishing connections between rate-distortion theory, minimum description length principles, and semantic concept discovery, we derive theoretical guarantees for representation optimality in multimedia content analysis tasks. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves sample complexity scaling of O(log N/N) for semantic concept acquisition, representing a significant theoretical improvement over conventional empirical bounds. Furthermore, we provide formal proofs establishing connections between information bottleneck principles and semantic fidelity metrics in visual and auditory modalities. The theoretical contributions include novel bounds on representation efficiency, conditions for optimal cross-modal alignment, and characterization of fundamental limits in semantic multimedia retrieval. This work establishes the first rigorous information-theoretic foundation bridging multimedia computing and semantic analysis, offering a paradigm shift from heuristic data-driven approaches toward theoretically grounded, interpretable, and sample-efficient semantic understanding systems.

Cross-modal retrieval in multimedia databases remains challenging due to inherent semantic gaps between different representation modalities, where existing embedding methods often fail to capture complex semantic correspondences. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of distribution alignment techniques for cross-modal retrieval, significantly improving upon conventional contrastive learning approaches through rigorous mathematical characterization. We formulate the cross-modal alignment problem using optimal transport theory and derive novel theoretical bounds that establish necessary and sufficient conditions for semantic correspondence preservation. Our analysis reveals that current contrastive objectives suffer from fundamental limitations arising from their inability to capture fine-grained semantic relationships, leading to mode collapse in high-dimensional embedding spaces. To address these deficiencies, we propose a Wasserstein-based alignment framework with theoretical guarantees on retrieval performance. We prove that our approach achieves minimax-optimal retrieval error rates under realistic assumptions about data distributions, improving upon existing generalization bounds by a factor proportional to the semantic concept manifold curvature. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets including MSCOCO and Flickr30k confirms the theoretical predictions, demonstrating substantial improvements in mean recall metrics. The theoretical contributions include novel concentration inequalities for cross-modal embeddings, characterization of semantic alignment complexity, and optimization landscape analysis for multimodal representation learning.

Traditional multimedia streaming architectures suffer from inherent limitations arising from their cloud-centric design, which struggles to satisfy the increasingly stringent requirements of latency-sensitive applications in dynamic network environments. This paper introduces EdgeCast, a novel edge-native streaming paradigm that fundamentally reimagines multimedia delivery through intelligent distribution of processing across network tiers. The system architecture comprises three innovative components: lightweight neural transcoders deployed at edge nodes, receiver-driven adaptive bitrate selection informed by edge-computed quality predictions, and a semantic-aware traffic engineering module for intelligent request routing. Unlike conventional approaches that centralize computational complexity at cloud datacenters, EdgeCast leverages in-network processing capabilities to enable real-time semantic enhancement without incurring prohibitive round-trip latencies. We design a hierarchical caching mechanism that exploits both temporal locality through conventional popularity-based strategies and semantic locality through learned concept embeddings, enabling efficient content reuse across heterogeneous user requests. The system implements novel quality-of-experience metrics that jointly optimize perceptual quality, buffering probability, and semantic fidelity. Implementation and evaluation across diverse network conditions including 5G testbeds and satellite links demonstrate that EdgeCast achieves 42% latency reduction while maintaining VMAF scores above 88, representing a fundamental shift toward edge intelligence in multimedia networking. The architecture provides graceful degradation under edge node failures through intelligent load balancing.

Existing multimedia retrieval systems face critical scalability challenges when attempting to balance retrieval speed with result quality in large-scale collections containing billions of items. Current approximate nearest neighbor methods based on inverted indices suffer from indexing overhead that scales poorly with feature dimensionality, while graph-based approaches incur prohibitive memory requirements. This paper presents ScaleSearch, a two-stage hierarchical retrieval system that significantly improves upon existing designs through novel integration of semantic hashing with graph-traversal refinement. The first stage employs learned binary hash codes computed via a transformer-based encoder trained with a novel triplet loss formulation that preserves both global similarity and local manifold structure. The second stage implements an optimized HNSW-based graph structure over the hashed representations, enabling efficient candidate refinement while dramatically reducing memory footprint. We introduce an adaptive early termination mechanism that dynamically adjusts the search budget based on query complexity estimation, further improving efficiency for simple queries while maintaining quality for complex semantic searches. The system includes a dynamic index update module supporting online insertion without full reconstruction, addressing the practical requirement for freshness in social multimedia applications. Comprehensive evaluation on datasets containing up to 100 million items demonstrates 4.2x speedup in mean query latency with less than 2% recall degradation compared to exhaustive search. The proposed design achieves linear memory scaling with collection size while maintaining sub-100ms retrieval times for 95th percentile queries.
